one_liner: Embeddable Lisp-family scripting language in one C99 file; roughly CPython speed, ahead only on interpreter-bound object and float code.
what_it_does: Janet is a small dynamic language with a bytecode compiler, a VM and a large core library (600+ functions: PEG parsing, a per-thread event loop, sockets, subprocesses, OS threads, a C FFI). You can run it as a standalone interpreter or embed it in a C or C++ program by compiling the amalgamated janet.c with janet.h and janetconf.h. It is not a drop-in for CPython: it is a different language with Lisp syntax, so adopting it means rewriting scripts.
how_it_is_fast: Janet compiles source to a compact register-based bytecode. On GCC and Clang the VM dispatches it with computed gotos (a switch elsewhere). Values are NaN-boxed into 8 bytes on x86-64, arm64 and riscv64, so numbers, nil and booleans need no heap allocation. The language discourages hash-table-heavy object orientation, which is the README's own explanation for any edge over Python. There is no JIT, and the GC is a simple stop-the-world collector.
when_to_use: Embedding a scripting or configuration layer in a C or C++ application, where one MIT-licensed C99 file is easier to vendor than CPython.
Interpreter-bound scripts that build many small trees or tuples, or do scalar float loops (binarytrees 1.55x and nbody 2.15x faster than CPython 3.8 in the only independent run).
Text parsing that fits a PEG grammar better than a regex, using the built-in PEG engine.
Scripts that need networking, subprocesses or OS threads from the core library without third-party packages.
when_not_to_use: As a speed upgrade over Python in general: the independent run has Janet about 1.12x slower than CPython 3.8 by geometric mean, and current CPython 3.11+ releases are faster than 3.8.
Byte-string, regex or big-integer heavy work: it lost reverse-complement 4.9x, pidigits 1.5x and regexredux 1.2x to CPython's C-implemented builtins, and the core has no regex engine or bignum type.
When raw interpreter speed decides: Lua 5.4 beat it on 4 of 5 shared benchmarks (about 1.43x geomean, derived from page data), and LuaJIT is far faster.
Latency-sensitive hosts with large heaps: the stop-the-world GC has no incremental mode yet (issue #1844 is open).
C++ hosts that rely on destructors during error propagation: Janet uses setjmp/longjmp for non-local returns.

integration.form: source-drop (amalgamated janet.c + janet.h + janetconf.h); also static or shared library and standalone binary via GNU make, Meson or build_win (MSVC)
integration.dependencies: libm; libdl only for dynamic native modules (-DJANET_NO_DYNAMIC_MODULES removes it); optional companions spork and jpm
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler (-std=c99); GNU make, Meson or Visual Studio build tools
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, illumos, 32-bit Haiku; NaN-boxing on x86-64, arm64 and riscv64, wider 12- or 16-byte values elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: VM state is thread-local: each OS thread runs its own VM with an isolated heap and GC, and data shared between threads is reference counted (README FAQ); a single VM must not be used from several threads

gotchas: Harness flaws in the only timing evidence (MikeBeller/janet-benchmarksgame): one run per benchmark, CPU time from /usr/bin/time, and runbench.janet checks only the exit code, never the output. The knucleotide outputs differ in format and sort order between the Janet and Python programs. The programs are also not like for like. Janet's revcomp2 caches translations of 6-byte windows. Its pidigits uses the third-party big (libbf) module with repeated-subtraction division. Its regexredux uses a hand-written regex-to-PEG converter and calls (gcsetinterval 1000000000), which effectively defers garbage collection. The Python regexredux still runs its matching through a one-worker multiprocessing Pool, despite the notebook's 'single threaded' note.

The measured Janet was built with -O2 -flto, and the benchmark repo says LTO cuts run time by up to 30%. Janet's default Makefile build does not enable LTO; issue #1904, opened 2026-10-06, proposes making it the default. Expect stock builds to be slower than the published numbers.
The evidence is dated: Janet 1.14.1 (2021) against today's 1.42.1 (2026-09-10) and 1.43.0-dev master, and Anaconda CPython 3.8 against current CPython. Nobody has measured the current standing.
Non-local exits use setjmp/longjmp (README FAQ), so a Janet error unwinding through C++ frames skips destructors; catch errors at the C boundary (for example with janet_pcall) in C++ hosts.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Janet over Wren or pocketpy when you want a larger standard library (PEG, event loop, networking, threads, FFI) in one embeddable C file and can accept CPython-class speed. Wren has the stronger measured lead over Lua 5.4 and Python 3.11, and pocketpy keeps Python syntax at about 1.2x CPython 3.8 on primes. Pick LuaJIT when throughput matters more than language features.
verified_claims_summary: The project publishes no numbers; its README FAQ says only 'a bit faster' than Python and 'YMMV'. The one independent run (MikeBeller/janet-benchmarksgame, 2021, Intel Core i5-7500 with hyperthreading off, single run, user+sys CPU seconds) timed Janet 1.14.1 built with -O2 -flto (C compiler unnamed) against Anaconda CPython 3.8. Janet was faster on binarytrees (1.55x), knucleotide (1.20x) and nbody (2.15x) and slower on fannkuch (1.04x), reverse-complement (4.9x), pidigits (1.53x) and regexredux (1.17x), about 1.12x slower by geometric mean (derived from page data).
status_note: Actively maintained (commits on 2026-10-06, release 1.42.1 on 2026-09-10) and MIT-licensed, easy to vendor as one C file; list it as an embeddable language with CPython-level speed, not as a faster replacement for CPython.
